ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Consider a thin rigid wire-frame MNPP'N'M' in which MNN'M' and NPP'N' are two squares of side $L$ with resistance per unit-length $\lambda$ and their planes are perpendicular. The frame is rotated with a constant angular velocity $\omega$ around an axis passing through $\mathrm{NN}$ ' and put in a region with constant magnetic field $B$ pointing perpendicular to $\mathrm{NN}^{\prime}$. What is the total heat released on the frame per revolution (in Joules)? Use $L=1 \mathrm{~m}, \lambda=1 \Omega / \mathrm{m}, \omega=2 \pi \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$ and $B=1 \mathrm{~T}$.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot:
Image description: The figure shows that the rigid wire frame is composed of left and right two square faces, the left face is MNN'M', the right face is NPP'N', and the geometric edge shared by the two squares is NN'. The green dashed line passes through N and N', indicating the rotation axis around the NN' direction, marked with angular velocity ω. The red arrow B indicates the direction of the uniform magnetic field, and is perpendicular to NN'. The actual wire contour is the outer boundary MNPP'N'M'; in the figure, NN' is the position of the rotation axis/common edge, not a segment of the actual closed wire. Reasoning: Take the spanning surface made by the two square faces MNN'M' and NPP'N' as the spanning surface of the closed wire MNPP'N'M'. The side lengths of the two squares are both L, the areas are both L^2, and the normal vectors of the two faces are perpendicular to each other. The wire frame rotates around NN' with angular velocity ω, while the magnetic field B is perpendicular to NN', so the magnetic fluxes of the two square faces differ by 90° in phase with time. The total magnetic flux can be written as Φ = B L^2(cos(ωt) ± sin(ωt)); the sign only depends on the convention of the area direction and does not affect the average power. According to Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction, the induced electromotive force on the closed wire is ε = -dΦ/dt. Since cos and sin in Φ differ by one quarter of a period, after taking the time average of the square, one obtains <ε^2> = B^2 L^4 ω^2. The actual wire length is six edges, with total length 6L, so the total resistance is R = 6λL. The average Joule power is

= <ε^2>/R = B^2 L^4 ω^2/(6λL). The time for one revolution is T = 2π/ω, so the heat released per revolution is Q =

T = [B^2 L^4 ω^2/(6λL)](2π/ω) = π B^2 L^3 ω/(3λ). Substituting L = 1 m, λ = 1 Ω/m, B = 1 T, ω = 2π rad/s: Q = π·1^2·1^3·(2π)/(3·1) = 2π^2/3 ≈ 6.58 J.

method.method_draft:
Use Faraday’s law on a convenient spanning surface made of the two square faces whose common edge would be NN'. From the image, read that NN' is the rotation axis, the right square NPP'N' and the left square MNN'M' are perpendicular, and the actual conducting frame is the outer six-sided wire MNPP'N'M' with no conducting segment along NN'. From the text, use side length L, resistance per unit length λ, angular speed ω, and uniform B perpendicular to the axis. Let the two square area vectors remain perpendicular during rotation, so their magnetic fluxes are phase-shifted by 90 degrees: Φ = B L^2(cos ωt ± sin ωt), up to sign convention. Then the induced emf around the single closed wire is ε = -dΦ/dt, whose mean square over one revolution is <ε^2> = B^2 L^4 ω^2. The total wire length is 6L, so R = 6λL. Average Joule power is

= <ε^2>/R, and heat per revolution is Q =

(2π/ω) = π B^2 L^3 ω/(3λ). Substituting L=1, λ=1, B=1, ω=2π gives Q = 2π^2/3 ≈ 6.58 J.

method.method_draft: Compute the motional emf directly from the line integral ε = ∮(v × B)·dl around the actual conducting wire. From the image, take NN' as the rotation axis and note that the loop path is M→N→P→P'→N'→M'→M, with two outer vertical edges PP' and M'M at distance L from the axis and two radial pairs connecting them to N and N'. From the text, use side L, uniform B perpendicular to the axis, and angular speed ω. Choose the axis as z and B along x. During rotation, a point at radius ρ and azimuth φ has v = ω zhat × r, giving (v×B)·zhat = -Bωρ cos φ. The radial horizontal pieces have dl perpendicular to v×B and contribute zero; only the two vertical outer edges contribute. Their azimuths differ by 90 degrees, so the net emf has the form ε(t)=BωL^2(cosωt ± sinωt), with sign depending on loop orientation. Hence <ε^2>=B^2ω^2L^4. The resistance of the six wire segments is R=6λL. Integrate Joule power over one period: Q=∫0^{2π/ω} ε(t)^2/R dt = πB^2L^3ω/(3λ). With L=λ=B=1 and ω=2π, Q≈6.58 J.
method.CoT_raw:
图像描述：图中绿色虚线穿过 N 和 N'，表示转轴 NN'；红色箭头 B 与该轴垂直。黑色导线构成非共面的六边形路径 M→N→P→P'→N'→M'→M，其中右侧方形 NPP'N' 与左侧方形 MNN'M' 的平面互相垂直。外侧竖直边 PP' 和 M'M 距转轴 NN' 的距离均为 L，两者所在方位相差 90°。

推理：按指定方法直接计算运动电动势 ε=∮(v×B)·dl。取 NN' 为 z 轴，磁场 B 沿 x 方向。转动时，半径为 ρ、方位角为 φ 的点速度为 v=ω zhat×r，因此 (v×B)·zhat=-Bωρ cosφ。水平径向导线段的 dl 在横向平面内，与 v×B 的 z 向分量垂直，所以不贡献电动势；只有两条外侧竖直边 PP' 和 M'M 有贡献。两条外侧边距轴均为 L，且方位角相差 90°，于是总电动势可写为 ε(t)=BωL^2(cosωt±sinωt)，符号取决于绕行方向，但对平方平均无影响。因此一周期内 <ε^2>=B^2ω^2L^4。导线总共有 6 段，每段长度 L，单位长度电阻为 λ，所以总电阻 R=6λL。每转释放热量 Q=∫0^(2π/ω) ε(t)^2/R dt = [B^2ω^2L^4/(6λL)]·[2π/ω] = πB^2L^3ω/(3λ)。代入 L=1 m、λ=1 Ω/m、B=1 T、ω=2π rad/s，得到 Q=2π^2/3≈6.58 J。

planner_metadata.text_role: Supplies the numerical values and confirms the side length, resistance per unit length, constant angular speed, and uniform magnetic field.
planner_metadata.knowledge_role: Use motional emf ε = ∮(v×B)·dl for a rigid conductor in a magnetic field, rotational velocity v = ω×r, Ohm/Joule law P = ε^2/R, and integration over one period.

raw_record.original_question: Consider a thin rigid wire-frame MNPP'N'M' in which MNN'M' and NPP'N' are two squares of side $L$ with resistance per unit-length $\lambda$ and their planes are perpendicular. The frame is rotated with a constant angular velocity $\omega$ around an axis passing through $\mathrm{NN}'$ and put in a region with constant magnetic field $B$ pointing perpendicular to $\mathrm{NN}'$. What is the total heat released on the frame per revolution (in Joules)? Use $L=1 \mathrm{~m}, \lambda=1 \Omega / \mathrm{m}, \omega=2 \pi \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$ and $B=1 \mathrm{~T}$.
raw_record.final_cot:
Image description: The figure shows that the rigid wire frame is composed of left and right two square faces, the left face is MNN'M', the right face is NPP'N', and the geometric edge shared by the two squares is NN'. The green dashed line passes through N and N', indicating the rotation axis around the NN' direction, marked with angular velocity ω. The red arrow B indicates the direction of the uniform magnetic field, and is perpendicular to NN'. The actual wire contour is the outer boundary MNPP'N'M'; in the figure, NN' is the position of the rotation axis/common edge, not a segment of the actual closed wire. Reasoning: Take the spanning surface made by the two square faces MNN'M' and NPP'N' as the spanning surface of the closed wire MNPP'N'M'. The side lengths of the two squares are both L, the areas are both L^2, and the normal vectors of the two faces are perpendicular to each other. The wire frame rotates around NN' with angular velocity ω, while the magnetic field B is perpendicular to NN', so the magnetic fluxes of the two square faces differ by 90° in phase with time. The total magnetic flux can be written as Φ = B L^2(cos(ωt) ± sin(ωt)); the sign only depends on the convention of the area direction and does not affect the average power. According to Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction, the induced electromotive force on the closed wire is ε = -dΦ/dt. Since cos and sin in Φ differ by one quarter of a period, after taking the time average of the square, one obtains <ε^2> = B^2 L^4 ω^2. The actual wire length is six edges, with total length 6L, so the total resistance is R = 6λL. The average Joule power is

= <ε^2>/R = B^2 L^4 ω^2/(6λL). The time for one revolution is T = 2π/ω, so the heat released per revolution is Q =

T = [B^2 L^4 ω^2/(6λL)](2π/ω) = π B^2 L^3 ω/(3λ). Substituting L = 1 m, λ = 1 Ω/m, B = 1 T, ω = 2π rad/s: Q = π·1^2·1^3·(2π)/(3·1) = 2π^2/3 ≈ 6.58 J.

critic_agent_reviews.critic_suggestions: The reasoning trace is consistent with the problem, image, standard answer, and assigned method draft. It correctly describes the image before reasoning, identifies NN' as the rotation axis/common geometric edge rather than a conducting segment, uses the two square spanning surfaces, derives the phase-shifted fluxes, computes the mean-square emf, uses total wire length 6L for resistance, and obtains 6.58 J. No substantive revision is needed.
